title: Missing angle on a straight line
problem: Two adjacent angles on a straight line are 47° and x. Find x.
reasoning: A straight line is a half-turn, so adjacent angles on it are supplementary: their sum is 180°.
steps: Identify the relationship: the two angles lie on one straight line.
interpretation: The unknown angle is obtuse. The diagram and the equation agree: the two angles complete a half-turn.
caption: Figure 7.1 · The two angles share a vertex and lie on a straight line.

title: Angles around a point
problem: Four angles meet at a point: 95°, 120°, 85° and x. Find x.
reasoning: A full turn around a point is 360°. The four angles must fill the turn exactly.
steps: Subtract from the full turn: x = 360° − 300° = 60°.
interpretation: The missing sector is acute. The visual model shows why the total must be 360°, not 180°.
caption: Figure 7.2 · Four sectors fill one full turn.

title: Vertically opposite angles with algebra
problem: Two lines cross. Vertically opposite angles are labelled 3x + 10° and x + 50°. Find x and one adjacent angle.
reasoning: Vertically opposite angles are equal. Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary.
steps: Set the opposite angles equal: 3x + 10 = x + 50.
interpretation: The algebra confirms the visual symmetry: opposite sectors match, and neighbouring sectors complete a line.
caption: Figure 7.3 · Opposite angles are equal; adjacent angles sum to 180°.

title: Parallel-line angle chase
problem: Lines l and m are parallel. The marked angle is 68°. Find a, b and c.
reasoning: With parallel lines, alternate angles are equal, co-interior angles are supplementary, and corresponding angles are equal.
steps: a is alternate to 68°, so a = 68°.
b is co-interior with 68°, so b = 180° − 68° = 112°.
c corresponds to the 68° angle (both are in the lower-right position), so c = 68°.
interpretation: The transversal creates two angle families: 68° and 112°. Naming the relationship prevents guessing from appearance.
caption: Figure 7.5 · Parallel marks justify the angle relationships.

title: Exterior angle of a triangle
problem: An exterior angle of a triangle is 115°. One opposite interior angle is 48°. Find the other opposite interior angle and the adjacent interior angle.
reasoning: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. It is supplementary to the interior angle at the same vertex.
answer: Other opposite angle 67°; adjacent interior angle 65°.
interpretation: The exterior angle is larger than either opposite interior angle. The diagram shows which angles belong to the exterior-angle relationship.
caption: Figure 7.6 · The exterior angle is outside the triangle at the extended base.

title: Isosceles base angles
problem: An isosceles triangle has apex angle 40°. Find each base angle.
reasoning: Equal sides have equal opposite angles. The triangle angle sum is 180°.
steps: The tick marks show two equal sides, so the base angles are equal. Call each x.
interpretation: The equal-side marks are the evidence for equal base angles; the calculation then uses the angle sum.
caption: Figure 7.7 · Equal sides force equal base angles.

title: Why every triangle has angle sum 180°
problem: Use a line through the apex parallel to the base to explain why the angles of a triangle sum to 180°.
reasoning: Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal. Angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
steps: Draw a line through the apex parallel to the base.
The left base angle equals the left angle at the apex (alternate angles). The right base angle equals the right angle at the apex.
The three angles on the straight line through the apex are therefore the three triangle angles.
They sum to 180°, so the triangle angles sum to 180°.
answer: A + B + C = 180° for every triangle.
interpretation: This is a visual argument, not a measurement of one triangle. It explains why the rule is general.
caption: Figure 7.8 · The parallel line transfers the base angles to the apex.

title: Missing angle in a quadrilateral
problem: A quadrilateral has angles 85°, 95°, 110° and x. Find x.
reasoning: A quadrilateral can be split into two triangles, so its interior angle sum is 2 × 180° = 360°.
interpretation: The diagonal in the diagram shows where the 360° comes from: two triangle sums.
caption: Figure 7.10 · One diagonal divides the quadrilateral into two triangles.

title: Regular polygon from an exterior angle
problem: A regular polygon has exterior angle 40°. Find the number of sides and each interior angle.
reasoning: The exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360°. In a regular polygon they are equal. Interior and exterior angles at a vertex are supplementary.
steps: Check with the interior-sum formula: (9 − 2) × 180° = 1260°, and 1260° ÷ 9 = 140°.
interpretation: A small exterior angle means many sides. The polygon is a regular nonagon.
caption: Figure 7.11 · A regular nonagon has nine equal exterior turns.

title: Possible third sides
problem: Two sides of a triangle are 7 cm and 11 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. Find all possible values.
reasoning: The third side must be greater than the difference of the other two sides and less than their sum. Endpoints give degenerate cases.
steps: Check endpoints: x = 4 gives 4 + 7 = 11; x = 18 gives 7 + 11 = 18. Both are straight-line cases, not triangles.
interpretation: The open circles on the number line show that 4 and 18 are excluded. The integer dots are the possible whole-centimetre lengths.
caption: Figure 7.13 · The number line represents 4 < x < 18.

title: Perpendicular bisector
problem: Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB = 8 cm. State the midpoint length and the check.
reasoning: Points on the perpendicular bisector are equidistant from A and B. Equal-radius arcs locate two such points.
steps: Choose one radius greater than half of AB, for example 5 cm. Keep it fixed.
Draw arcs from A and from B above and below AB. Label the intersections P and Q.
Draw PQ. It crosses AB at its midpoint M, so AM = MB = 4 cm, and PQ is perpendicular to AB.
answer: AM = MB = 4 cm; PQ is perpendicular to AB.
interpretation: The arcs are evidence: P and Q are each the same distance from A and B, so the line through them is the perpendicular bisector.
caption: Figure 7.15 · The same compass radius is used from both endpoints.

title: Angle bisector
problem: Bisect a 64° angle with ruler and compasses. Find each half.
reasoning: An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal angles. Equal-radius arcs from the arms locate a point on the bisector.
steps: Draw an arc from the vertex O, cutting the arms at P and Q.
With the same radius from P and Q, draw arcs meeting at R.
Draw OR. This is the angle bisector.
interpretation: The construction forces equality; measuring is only a check. Do not confuse this with the perpendicular bisector of a segment.
caption: Figure 7.16 · The bisector is the ray OR.

title: Triangle from three sides (SSS)
problem: Construct a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm.
reasoning: If two sides and the base are fixed, the third vertex is the intersection of two circles/arcs. The triangle inequality predicts whether the arcs meet.
steps: Check: 5 + 6 > 7, so a triangle is possible.
From A draw an arc of radius 5 cm; from B draw an arc of radius 6 cm.
Label the intersection C and join AC and BC. Keep the arcs visible.
answer: Triangle ABC has AB = 7 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm.
interpretation: The arcs locate the only possible apex on each side of the base. The two choices are mirror images.
caption: Figure 7.17 · The arc intersection fixes the third vertex.

title: Isosceles triangle and a locus
problem: Construct an isosceles triangle with equal sides 6 cm and base 8 cm. Explain why the perpendicular bisector of the base passes through the apex.
reasoning: The apex is equidistant from the base endpoints. The perpendicular bisector is the locus of all points equidistant from the endpoints.
steps: With radius 6 cm from A and from B, draw arcs meeting at C.
Join AC and BC. Then AC = BC = 6 cm.
Because C is equidistant from A and B, it lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
answer: The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through C.
interpretation: The equal sides are not just a picture feature; they place the apex on a precise locus. This connects construction with reasoning.
caption: Figure 7.18 · Equal sides place the apex on the perpendicular bisector.
